pos: v. (archaic past tense of sling; hurled from a sling)
etymology: The old strong past tense of sling, formed like sing/sang and ring/rang. The Hebrew verb is qala, to sling or hurl a stone. It has nothing to do with the modern noun slang meaning low or casual speech, which arose in the eighteenth century, long after 1611.
biblical_def: One word in the Authorized Version carries the whole weight of the most famous single combat in Scripture: “And David put his hand in his bag, and took thence a stone, and slang it, and smote the Philistine in his forehead, that the stone sunk into his forehead; and he fell upon his face to the earth” (1 Samuel 17:49). Slang is the past tense of sling, and it is the only occurrence of that form in the whole English Bible. The verse is deliberately plain. No lightning, no angelic host, no miracle described in the telling; a shepherd's hand, a bag, a stone, and a sling. The theology was already spoken before the stone flew: “I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied” (1 Samuel 17:45), and “the battle is the LORD'S” (1 Samuel 17:47). The LORD who had taught David's hand against the lion and the bear in the obscurity of the sheepfold had been preparing the stroke for years. Grace does not despise ordinary means. It governs them. The stone went where providence sent it, and the giant fell on his face toward the earth he had boasted over. “The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD” (Proverbs 21:31).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SLANG, the past tense of sling; to throw with a sling, to hurl, to cast.
webster_full: SLANG, the past tense of SLING; now commonly slung.
SLING, v.t. To throw with a sling; to hurl; to cast.
To hang so as to swing; as, to sling a pack.
1 Samuel 17:49 is the only place the form slang appears in the Authorized Version.
The modern noun slang, meaning low speech, is a later and unrelated word.
scriptures: And David put his hand in his bag, and took thence a stone, and slang it, and smote the Philistine in his forehead, that the stone sunk into his forehead; and he fell upon his face to the earth.

Then said David to the Philistine, Thou comest to me with a sword, and with a spear, and with a shield: but I come to thee in the name of the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom thou hast defied.
The horse is prepared against the day of battle: but safety is of the LORD.
corruption_summary: The duel is retold as a parable of self-belief, the underdog who wins by daring greatly, with the name of the LORD of hosts quietly removed from the story.
corruption_paragraphs: David and Goliath has become the stock illustration of the plucky underdog, the small competitor who beats the market leader, the believer in himself who refuses to be told the odds. In that retelling the sling is skill, the stone is strategy, and the lesson is that the giants in your life are smaller than they look. Every element of the account survives except the only one David himself named: the LORD of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel.

Scripture will not permit that reading. David announces before he throws that the LORD saves not with sword and spear, and that the whole assembly will learn it. The stone is not David's confidence; it is God's instrument. Recover the plain sense and the comfort grows rather than shrinks: the believer facing a real giant is not told to find courage in himself, but to come in the name of the LORD, and to leave the outcome where it has always lain.
roots_summary: Old strong past tense of sling; Hebrew qala, to hurl with a sling; 1 Samuel 17:49 is the sole occurrence.
roots_lines: Slang is the old strong past tense of sling, on the pattern sing/sang.
Hebrew qala, to sling or hurl a stone.
1 Samuel 17:49 is the only occurrence of the form in the Authorized Version.
The modern noun slang, low or casual speech, is an unrelated eighteenth-century word.
The stroke is reported without a miracle, yet the whole battle was the LORD'S.
usage: and took thence a stone, and slang it
marks the ordinary means by which God gave an extraordinary victory
preserves the old strong past tense that modern versions replace with slung

pos: n. (archaic; an occurrence, an event befalling one, a mischance)
etymology: From Latin occurrere, to run against, to meet, to befall, from ob (against) and currere (to run). In 1611 English an occurrent was a thing that ran against you, an event that came to meet you unbidden.
biblical_def: Solomon, writing to Hiram king of Tyre about building the temple, describes the peace God has given him: “But now the LORD my God hath given me rest on every side, so that there is neither adversary nor evil occurrent” (1 Kings 5:4). An occurrent is an occurrence, an event that runs to meet a man; an evil occurrent is a mischance, an untoward happening, the kind of thing that disrupts a reign and postpones a building. Solomon names two things absent from his kingdom: no adversary, meaning no human enemy at the gate, and no evil occurrent, meaning no disaster from any other quarter. The word therefore testifies to a doctrine larger than itself. Occurrences are not loose. They do not simply run against a kingdom; they are given or withheld by the LORD, who “worketh all things after the counsel of his own will” (Ephesians 1:11). David had been denied the building because of war; Solomon received it because the LORD had granted rest on every side. The temple rose in a window of peace that God Himself opened, and Solomon knew whose hand held it open: “I purpose to build an house unto the name of the LORD my God” (1 Kings 5:5).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): OCCURRENT, n. an incident; any thing that happens; an occurrence.
webster_full: OCCURRENT, n. An incident; any thing that happens.
OCCURRENT, a. Occurring; meeting; coming in the way.
From Latin occurrere, to run against, to meet, to befall.
1 Kings 5:4 speaks of neither adversary nor evil occurrent.
The noun has fallen out of use; occurrence replaced it.
scriptures: But now the LORD my God hath given me rest on every side, so that there is neither adversary nor evil occurrent.

And, behold, I purpose to build an house unto the name of the LORD my God, as the LORD spake unto David my father, saying, Thy son, whom I will set upon thy throne in thy room, he shall build an house unto my name.
Eph 1:11
In whom also we have obtained an inheritance, being predestinated according to the purpose of him who worketh all things after the counsel of his own will:
corruption_summary: Events are treated as genuinely random, so that chance and not God becomes the explanation of what befalls a man, a family or a nation.
corruption_paragraphs: The modern mind has a settled category for the evil occurrent: bad luck. Accident, coincidence, random chance, the universe being indifferent. On that account an evil occurrent is exactly what the word's Latin root pictures and nothing more, a thing that happened to run into you, with no hand behind it and no meaning in it. Insurance calls such events acts of God while meaning precisely that no one is responsible.

Scripture grants no autonomous realm of chance. The lot, the arrow shot at a venture, the sparrow's fall and the hair of the head are all under the decree. Solomon does not thank fortune for the absence of evil occurrents; he says the LORD his God hath given him rest on every side. The doctrine comforts rather than crushes: if nothing runs against the believer except by the counsel of God's own will, then nothing that runs against him is wasted.
roots_summary: Latin occurrere, to run against or befall; 1 Kings 5:4 is the sole occurrence, denying any mischance in Solomon's realm.
roots_lines: Latin ob, against, and currere, to run: occurrere, to run against, to befall.
An occurrent is an occurrence; an evil occurrent is a mischance.
1 Kings 5:4 is the only occurrence in the Authorized Version.
Solomon names two absences: no adversary, and no evil occurrent.
The rest that allowed the temple to be built was given by the LORD.
usage: neither adversary nor evil occurrent
names the mischance that God withheld from Solomon's reign
witnesses against any doctrine of autonomous chance

pos: v. (archaic spelling of jostle; to run or push against, to collide)
etymology: A frequentative of joust, from Old French jouster, to tilt or run against in combat, ultimately Latin iuxta, near. Justle is the older spelling; jostle is the modern. The Hebrew shaqaq pictures running to and fro in confusion.
biblical_def: Nahum is describing the fall of Nineveh, and the picture is of chariots in panic: “The chariots shall rage in the streets, they shall justle one against another in the broad ways: they shall seem like torches, they shall run like the lightnings” (Nahum 2:4). To justle is to run and push against, to collide in a crowd. The word is exactly right for the thing described. These are not chariots in formation but chariots in rout, crashing into one another in the very broad ways that were built for their parade. Nineveh's military glory becomes Nineveh's military chaos, and the speed that terrified the nations now only hastens the city's own ruin. Nahum has already given the reason: “Woe to the bloody city! it is all full of lies and robbery; the prey departeth not” (Nahum 3:1). The same prophecy that pronounces Nineveh's doom holds out a refuge: “The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him” (Nahum 1:7). The justling chariots are the picture of every power that has nothing to stand on but its own momentum.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): JUSTLE, to run against; to push; to drive or force by running against.
webster_full: JUSTLE, v.i. To run against; to encounter; to clash.
JUSTLE, v.t. To push; to drive; to force by rushing against.
A frequentative of joust, to tilt or run against in combat.
Nahum 2:4 pictures chariots justling one against another in Nineveh's broad ways.
The spelling jostle has since replaced it.
scriptures: Nah 2:4
The chariots shall rage in the streets, they shall justle one against another in the broad ways: they shall seem like torches, they shall run like the lightnings.
Nah 3:1
Woe to the bloody city! it is all full of lies and robbery; the prey departeth not;
Nah 1:7
The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.
corruption_summary: The fall of a cruel empire is read as mere geopolitics, the natural cycle of rising and declining powers, with the moral verdict of God on blood and robbery edited out.
corruption_paragraphs: Nineveh's collapse is routinely explained as the ordinary life-cycle of empire: overextension, imperial fatigue, a coalition of rivals, the usual pattern. The explanation is not false as far as it goes, and Scripture never denies secondary causes. What it refuses is the reduction. On the purely political account the justling chariots mean nothing beyond the mechanics of a rout.

Nahum names the cause above the causes. This is the bloody city, full of lies and robbery, and the LORD is the one who makes an utter end of her place. The prophecy is addressed to Judah for comfort: the empire that seemed eternal is already judged, and the LORD is a strong hold in the day of trouble to them that trust in Him. Every power whose momentum is its only foundation will one day justle against itself in its own broad ways.
roots_summary: Older spelling of jostle, from joust, to run against; Nahum 2:4 pictures Nineveh's chariots colliding in her own streets.
roots_lines: A frequentative of joust, Old French jouster, to run against in combat.
Hebrew shaqaq, to run to and fro, to rush about in confusion.
Nahum 2:4 is the only occurrence in the Authorized Version.
The broad ways built for parade become the place of the rout.
Nahum 1:7 sets a strong hold over against the justling chariots.
usage: they shall justle one against another in the broad ways
pictures the self-collision of a doomed military power
preserves the older spelling of jostle

pos: v. (past tense; hazarded, exposed to deadly risk)
etymology: From Old French jeu parti, a divided game, an even chance, hence a hazard. Jeopard is the older verb, now displaced by jeopardize. The Hebrew charaph here means to expose or cast down, to despise one's own life for a cause.
biblical_def: In the song of Deborah the tribes are reviewed one by one, and the honour roll is short: “Zebulun and Naphtali were a people that jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field” (Judges 5:18). To jeopard a life is to put it at even hazard, to throw it where it may well be lost. Zebulun and Naphtali came down to Kishon when Barak called, and the song does not praise their success but their willingness to die. Set against them stands Meroz: “Curse ye Meroz, said the angel of the LORD, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof; because they came not to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty” (Judges 5:23). The dividing line in the song is not between brave men and cowards in the abstract but between those who answered the LORD's call at cost and those who stayed by their flocks and ships. The whole principle is gathered up and perfected in Christ, who did not merely jeopard His life but laid it down: “Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): JEOPARD, to hazard; to put in danger; to expose to loss or injury.
webster_full: JEOPARD, v.t. To hazard; to put in danger; to expose to loss or injury.
JEOPARDY, n. Exposure to death, loss or injury; hazard; danger; peril.
From Old French jeu parti, a divided or even game, hence a hazard.
Judges 5:18 praises Zebulun and Naphtali, who jeoparded their lives unto the death.
The form jeoparded has been displaced by jeopardized.
scriptures: Jdg 5:18
Zebulun and Naphtali were a people that jeoparded their lives unto the death in the high places of the field.
Jdg 5:23
Curse ye Meroz, said the angel of the LORD, curse ye bitterly the inhabitants thereof; because they came not to the help of the LORD, to the help of the LORD against the mighty.
Greater love hath no man than this, that a man lay down his life for his friends.
corruption_summary: Costly obedience is downgraded to a lifestyle option, so that the believer who risks nothing is told he is simply honouring his own boundaries.
corruption_paragraphs: A church shaped by the vocabulary of self-care has little room for a people that jeoparded their lives unto the death. Risk is reframed as poor stewardship of the self, and the refusal to come down to the battle is dignified as the setting of a healthy limit. Meroz is no longer cursed; Meroz is commended for knowing its own capacity.

Scripture keeps the harder categories. The angel of the LORD curses the tribe that stayed home, and the song honours the tribes that went. The call is not to recklessness, and the believer owes real duties to family and calling; but Deborah's song and the cross together forbid the doctrine that a Christian owes God nothing he is unwilling to lose. He who laid down His life for His friends has every right to ask the risk of His people.
roots_summary: From jeu parti, an even game or hazard; Judges 5:18 honours the tribes that hazarded their lives unto the death.
roots_lines: Old French jeu parti, a divided game, an even chance, hence a hazard.
Hebrew charaph here means to expose or despise one's own life for a cause.

pos: n. pl. (those who strike; men who beat another with blows)
etymology: From Old English smitan, to smear, strike or beat. The agent noun smiter is one who smites. The Hebrew in Isaiah 50:6 is nakah, to strike or beat.
biblical_def: The third Servant song puts the words in the Servant's own mouth: “I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting” (Isaiah 50:6). The smiters are the men with the rods and the scourge, and the verb gave is the heart of the verse. The Servant is not seized and overpowered; He surrenders His back. Seven centuries before the praetorium Isaiah had written the Gospel passion narrative in the first person, and the Evangelists record the fulfilment detail by detail: the scourging, the plucked beard, the spitting, the mockery. The Servant is the Lord Jesus Christ, and His submission to the smiters was not weakness but priestly action: “But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed” (Isaiah 53:5). Peter, who watched it, draws the pastoral conclusion for a suffering church: “Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously” (1 Peter 2:23).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SMITER, he that smites; one who strikes or beats.
webster_full: SMITER, n. He that smites or strikes.
SMITE, v.t. To strike; to throw, drive or force against, as the fist or hand.
To kill; to destroy the life of by beating or by weapons.
To afflict; to chasten; to punish.
Isaiah 50:6 says the Servant gave His back to the smiters.
scriptures: Isa 50:6
I gave my back to the smiters, and my cheeks to them that plucked off the hair: I hid not my face from shame and spitting.
Isa 53:5
But he was wounded for our transgressions, he was bruised for our iniquities: the chastisement of our peace was upon him; and with his stripes we are healed.
Who, when he was reviled, reviled not again; when he suffered, he threatened not; but committed himself to him that judgeth righteously:
corruption_summary: The Servant songs are detached from Christ and read as the voice of the nation only, so that the scourging becomes an example of endurance rather than a substitutionary suffering for sin.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern academic treatment of Isaiah 40 to 55 regularly assigns the Servant songs to Israel collectively or to an unnamed prophet of the exile, and divides the book among a Deutero- and Trito-Isaiah on the way. The dictionary rejects both moves. There is one prophet Isaiah, and the New Testament settles the identification of the Servant: Philip opened Isaiah 53 to the eunuch and preached Jesus from it.

What hangs on it is the atonement. If the smiters merely struck a suffering nation, then Isaiah 50 teaches resilience. If they struck the incarnate Son who gave them His back, then the stripes are penal and substitutionary, borne for transgressions not His own, and the believer's healing is purchased rather than illustrated. The whole comfort of the passage rests on the Person who was struck.
roots_summary: Agent noun from Old English smitan, to strike; Isaiah 50:6 is the sole occurrence, spoken by the suffering Servant.
roots_lines: Old English smitan, to strike or beat; a smiter is one who strikes.
Hebrew nakah, to strike, beat or scourge.
Isaiah 50:6 is the only occurrence of the plural smiters in the Authorized Version.
The Servant gave His back; He was not merely overpowered.
Isaiah 53:5 names the stripes as penal and healing.

pos: v. (to surround, to encircle, to hem in on every side)
etymology: From Old French environner, to surround, from en (in) and viron (a circuit), related to virer, to turn. The Hebrew sabab means to go round about, to encircle.
biblical_def: After the defeat at Ai, Joshua lies on his face before the ark and pleads the honour of God's name: “For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land shall hear of it, and shall environ us round, and cut off our name from the earth: and what wilt thou do unto thy great name?” (Joshua 7:9). To environ is to surround, to close a ring about a thing. Joshua's fear is encirclement: a nation that has lost the field once will be hemmed in by every tribe in Canaan, and the name of the LORD will be the thing finally cut off. The answer he receives is not comfort but diagnosis: “Israel hath sinned, and they have also transgressed my covenant which I commanded them” (Joshua 7:11). Achan's hidden theft, not Canaanite numbers, had opened the breach. The word is worth keeping because Scripture turns it around in blessing: “As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever” (Psalm 125:2). There are two encirclements in the Bible. Sin exposes a people to the first; covenant mercy sets them within the second.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): ENVIRON, to surround; to encompass; to encircle; to hem in; to involve or envelop.
webster_full: ENVIRON, v.t. To surround; to encompass; to encircle.
To involve or envelop; as, to environ with darkness or with difficulties.
To besiege; to hem in with hostile forces.
From Old French environner, from en, in, and viron, a circuit.
Joshua 7:9 fears that the Canaanites will environ Israel round.
scriptures: Josh 7:9
For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land shall hear of it, and shall environ us round, and cut off our name from the earth: and what wilt thou do unto thy great name?
Josh 7:11

Israel hath sinned, and they have also transgressed my covenant which I commanded them: for they have even taken of the accursed thing, and have also stolen, and dissembled also, and they have put it even among their own stuff.
As the mountains are round about Jerusalem, so the LORD is round about his people from henceforth even for ever.
corruption_summary: Defeat in the church is diagnosed as external pressure from a hostile culture, when Scripture sends the leader first to look for the accursed thing within the camp.
corruption_paragraphs: When a congregation or a ministry suffers a reverse, the ready explanation is the surrounding environment: a hostile culture, a hard field, a post-Christian age, forces that environ the church on every side. The explanation flatters, because it locates the problem wholly outside the camp and makes the remedy a matter of strategy.

Joshua reasoned the same way and was corrected. The Canaanites had not grown stronger; Israel had sinned, and the accursed thing was hidden in a tent. The LORD would not hear the prayer until the camp was searched. The pattern governs the church still: repentance within precedes victory without, and the people whom God sets inside the encircling mountains of Psalm 125 are a people who have dealt with the sin in their own stuff.
roots_summary: Old French environner, to surround; Joshua 7:9 fears encirclement, and Psalm 125:2 answers with the LORD round about His people.
roots_lines: Old French environner, from en, in, and viron, a circuit.
Hebrew sabab, to go round about, to encircle.

pos: n. pl. (those who empty out; plunderers who strip a land bare)
etymology: Agent noun from empty, Old English aemtig, unoccupied, at leisure, hence void. The Hebrew baqaq means to pour out, to lay waste, to empty utterly.
biblical_def: Nahum turns from Nineveh to the comfort of Jacob and names the wound before he names the cure: “For the LORD hath turned away the excellency of Jacob, as the excellency of Israel: for the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches” (Nahum 2:2). The emptiers are the Assyrian plunderers, and the word is chosen for its thoroughness. They did not merely tax or raid; they emptied the land out, as a vessel is poured until nothing remains, and they marred the vine branches so that the next harvest was taken with this one. But the verse does not begin with Assyria. It begins with the LORD, who hath turned away the excellency of Jacob. The emptiers emptied because the LORD had first withdrawn His glory from a covenant-breaking people, and the chastening hand is His even when the instrument is pagan. The same prophet who says it also says the LORD will restore it, for the clause is grammatically the ground of a promise of return. Isaiah speaks the identical doctrine in the largest terms: “Behold, the LORD maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste” (Isaiah 24:1), and “The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked” (Nahum 1:3).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): EMPTIER, one who empties or exhausts; EMPTY, to pour out or make void.
webster_full: EMPTIER, n. One that empties or exhausts.
EMPTY, v.t. To exhaust; to make void or destitute; to deprive of the contents.
EMPTY, a. Containing nothing; void of the usual contents.
From Old English aemtig, unoccupied, void.
Nahum 2:2 says the emptiers have emptied Jacob out and marred their vine branches.
scriptures: Nah 2:2
For the LORD hath turned away the excellency of Jacob, as the excellency of Israel: for the emptiers have emptied them out, and marred their vine branches.
Nah 1:3
The LORD is slow to anger, and great in power, and will not at all acquit the wicked: the LORD hath his way in the whirlwind and in the storm, and the clouds are the dust of his feet.
Isa 24:1
Behold, the LORD maketh the earth empty, and maketh it waste, and turneth it upside down, and scattereth abroad the inhabitants thereof.
corruption_summary: Plunder and national calamity are read as pure victimhood, with the covenant hand of God in chastening denied, so that there is nothing to repent of and nothing to hope for.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors stand on either side of this verse. The first makes the plundered people simply innocent, a nation acted upon by stronger neighbours, with the whole account told in the vocabulary of oppression and nothing said of covenant. The second makes the plunderers simply instruments, excusing Assyrian cruelty because God used it.

Nahum refuses both. The LORD had turned away the excellency of Jacob, so Israel had something to repent of; and Nineveh is the bloody city whom God will not at all acquit, so Assyria had everything to answer for. Divine sovereignty over the emptiers never cancels their guilt, and the sin of the emptiers never cancels Israel's need of repentance. Hold both and the verse becomes what Nahum made it, the ground of a promise that the excellency turned away will be restored.
roots_summary: Agent noun from empty; Hebrew baqaq, to pour out utterly; Nahum 2:2 names Assyria the emptiers of Jacob.
roots_lines: Old English aemtig, unoccupied or void, gives empty and emptier.
Hebrew baqaq, to pour out, to lay waste, to empty utterly.

usage: the emptiers have emptied them out

pos: v. (archaic past participle of fold; entwined, matted together)
etymology: Old strong past participle of fold, Old English fealdan, on the pattern of stolen and broken. The Hebrew sabak means to interweave or entangle, as thorn bushes grow into one another.
biblical_def: Nahum's first chapter gathers Nineveh's strength into one image and burns it: “For while they be folden together as thorns, and while they are drunken as drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry” (Nahum 1:10). Folden is the old past participle of fold, here meaning entwined or matted, as a thicket of thorns grows into a single tangled mass that cannot be pulled apart. That interlocking is Nineveh's confidence. Her alliances, her garrisons, her fortified ring are folden together, and the tangle that no hand can unpick is precisely what makes her burn. Dry thorns matted together do not resist fire; they carry it. The prophet adds drunkenness to the picture, the carelessness of a city at its feast, and then speaks the sentence: devoured as stubble fully dry. Malachi uses the same figure of the last day: “all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble” (Malachi 4:1). The strength men weave for themselves becomes the fuel of the judgment they weave it against, while “the LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble” (Nahum 1:7).
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FOLD, to double; to lap or complain one part over another; to wrap or involve; folden is the old participle.
webster_full: FOLD, v.t. To double; to lap or lay in plaits; to wrap or involve.
To enclose; to shut in; as sheep in a fold.
FOLDEN is the old past participle, now displaced by folded.
Hebrew sabak, to interweave or entangle, as thorns.
Nahum 1:10 says Nineveh is folden together as thorns and shall be devoured as stubble.
scriptures: Nah 1:10
For while they be folden together as thorns, and while they are drunken as drunkards, they shall be devoured as stubble fully dry.
Nah 1:7
The LORD is good, a strong hold in the day of trouble; and he knoweth them that trust in him.
Mal 4:1

For, behold, the day cometh, that shall burn as an oven; and all the proud, yea, and all that do wickedly, shall be stubble: and the day that cometh shall burn them up, saith the LORD of hosts, that it shall leave them neither root nor branch.
corruption_summary: Interlocking human strength is trusted as though density were safety, when Scripture says a matted thicket of thorns is the readiest fuel for fire.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one Nahum presses: tangled strength is not security. Nineveh's walls, treaties and garrisons were folden together so tightly that no enemy could find a loose edge, and the prophet treats that very interlocking as the reason the city would burn fast.

The temptation is perennial and respectable. Institutions, including churches and ministries, weave redundancy and alliance until the structure seems unpickable, and mistake complexity for safety. Dry thorns matted together are not stronger against fire; they are better fuel. The only strong hold in the day of trouble is the LORD, who knoweth them that trust in Him.
roots_summary: Old strong participle of fold; Hebrew sabak, to entangle as thorns; Nahum 1:10 makes the tangle the fuel.
roots_lines: Old English fealdan, to fold; folden is its strong past participle.
Hebrew sabak, to interweave or entangle, used of thorn thickets.
Nahum 1:10 is the only occurrence of folden in the Authorized Version.
The tangle that resists unpicking is the thing that carries the fire.
Malachi 4:1 applies the stubble figure to the day of the LORD.
usage: while they be folden together as thorns
pictures interlocked human strength as fuel for judgment
preserves the old strong participle displaced by folded

pos: n. pl. (small fragments, splinters, pieces into which a brittle thing shatters)
etymology: From Middle English schivere, a splinter or fragment, related to Low German schever. To break a thing to shivers is to shatter it into slivers. The Greek in Revelation 2:27 is suntribo, to break in pieces, to crush.
biblical_def: To the overcomer in Thyatira the risen Christ grants a share in His own royal rule: “And he shall rule them with a rod of iron; as the vessels of a potter shall they be broken to shivers: even as I received of my Father” (Revelation 2:27). Shivers are splinters, the fragments left when a brittle vessel is dashed down. The promise is a quotation of the second Psalm, where the Father says to the Son, “Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel” (Psalm 2:9). Christ has received that authority from His Father, and He shares it with His overcoming saints, who will judge the world with Him. The figure is exact and sobering: unfired clay can be remade, but a hardened potter's vessel once dashed down cannot be mended, as Jeremiah was commanded to show at Tophet (Jeremiah 19:11). The nations that will not have the Son are not merely defeated; they are broken to shivers. The word therefore belongs to the dictionary's eschatology: final judgment is real, irreversible, and administered by the Lamb.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): SHIVER, a small piece or fragment into which a thing breaks by sudden violence.
webster_full: SHIVER, n. A small piece or fragment into which a thing breaks by any sudden violence.
SHIVER, v.t. To break into many small pieces, or splinters; to shatter.
To break to shivers is to shatter into slivers or splinters.
Greek suntribo, to break in pieces, to crush together.
Revelation 2:27 says the nations shall be broken to shivers as a potter's vessels.
scriptures: Rev 2:27
And he shall rule them with a rod of iron; as the vessels of a potter shall they be broken to shivers: even as I received of my Father.
Psa 2:9
Thou shalt break them with a rod of iron; thou shalt dash them in pieces like a potter's vessel.

And shalt say unto them, Thus saith the LORD of hosts; Even so will I break this people and this city, as one breaketh a potter's vessel, that cannot be made whole again: and they shall bury them in Tophet, till there be no place to bury.
corruption_summary: Final judgment is softened into eventual restoration for all, so that no vessel is finally broken and the rod of iron becomes a figure of speech.
corruption_paragraphs: Universalism in its old Origenist form and in its modern evangelical dress teaches that no one is finally lost, that the fire purges rather than punishes, and that what Scripture calls destruction is a long road home. Annihilationism takes the other road, agreeing that judgment is real but denying that it endures. Both deny what the broken potter's vessel says: Jeremiah was told to say of it that it cannot be made whole again.

The dictionary holds the confessional position: eternal conscious punishment of the unredeemed, final and irreversible, administered by Christ to whom the Father has given all judgment. The language of Revelation 2:27 is not decorative. It is the inheritance of the overcomer, and it is the warning of the gospel. The invitation to kiss the Son in Psalm 2 is urgent precisely because the rod of iron is not a metaphor for a second chance.
roots_summary: Middle English schivere, a splinter; Greek suntribo, to crush; Revelation 2:27 quotes Psalm 2:9 on the broken vessel.
roots_lines: Middle English schivere, a splinter or fragment.
Greek suntribo, to break in pieces, to crush together.
Revelation 2:27 is the only occurrence of broken to shivers in the Authorized Version.
The verse quotes Psalm 2:9 and grants the overcomer a share in Christ's rule.
Jeremiah 19:11 stresses that the broken vessel cannot be made whole again.
usage: as the vessels of a potter shall they be broken to shivers
names the irreversibility of final judgment
promises the overcomer a share in the rule of Christ

pos: n. (one who fells trees; a woodcutter, a hewer of timber)
etymology: Agent noun from fell, Old English fiellan, to cause to fall, the causative of fall. A feller is one who brings timber down. The Hebrew karath means to cut off or cut down.
biblical_def: Isaiah's taunt song over the fallen king of Babylon lets even the trees speak: “Yea, the fir trees rejoice at thee, and the cedars of Lebanon, saying, Since thou art laid down, no feller is come up against us” (Isaiah 14:8). A feller is a woodcutter. Assyrian and Babylonian kings boasted in their inscriptions of cutting the cedars of Lebanon for palaces and temples, and the prophet turns the boast into a dirge. The tyrant who felled forests is himself laid down, and the cedars he spared no longer hear the axe on the mountain. The irony is deepened by the same prophet's earlier word, where the LORD is the woodsman: “he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one” (Isaiah 10:34). Babylon felled Lebanon; God fells Babylon. And John the Baptist brings the figure to the conscience of every hearer: “And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire” (Matthew 3:10). There is always a feller coming up; the question is only whose hand holds the axe.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): FELLER, one who hews or knocks down; FELL, to cause to fall, as to fell trees.
webster_full: FELLER, n. One who hews or knocks down.
FELL, v.t. To cause to fall; to prostrate; to bring to the ground.
To cut down; as, to fell trees.
The causative of fall, Old English fiellan.
Isaiah 14:8 says the cedars rejoice that no feller is come up against them.
scriptures: Isa 14:8
Yea, the fir trees rejoice at thee, and the cedars of Lebanon, saying, Since thou art laid down, no feller is come up against us.
And he shall cut down the thickets of the forest with iron, and Lebanon shall fall by a mighty one.
Mat 3:10
And now also the axe is laid unto the root of the trees: therefore every tree which bringeth not forth good fruit is hewn down, and cast into the fire.
corruption_summary: Isaiah's taunt song is read as nothing but ancient political satire, and the axe laid to the root is softened into a general call to improvement rather than a warning of judgment.
corruption_paragraphs: Isaiah 14 is often handled as pure literary artifice, a genre piece whose business is to mock a dead king and nothing more. The prophecy is literature of the highest order, and the dictionary is glad to say so; but it is prophecy before it is poetry, and the taunt is uttered against a real tyrant by the real God who laid him down. The historical-critical instinct to date the chapter late and read it backward from events empties it of the very thing it claims, that the LORD declares the end from the beginning.

The corruption touches the hearer more nearly at Matthew 3:10. The axe laid unto the root is regularly preached as encouragement to bear more fruit, a gentle nudge toward growth. John the Baptist means something sharper: the tree that brings forth no good fruit is hewn down and cast into the fire. The feller is coming. The call is to repentance, and the fruit is its evidence, not its substitute.
roots_summary: Agent noun from fell, the causative of fall; Hebrew karath, to cut down; Isaiah 14:8 gives the cedars rest from the feller.
roots_lines: Old English fiellan, to cause to fall, the causative of fall.
Hebrew karath, to cut off or cut down.
Isaiah 14:8 is the only occurrence of feller in the Authorized Version.
Babylonian kings boasted of felling the cedars of Lebanon.
Isaiah 10:34 makes the LORD Himself the woodsman against Lebanon.
usage: no feller is come up against us
names the woodcutter whose axe the cedars feared
turns a tyrant's boast into his dirge
